source: Ellamil, Dobson, Beeman, Christoff (2012) Evaluative and generative modes of thought during the creative process. NeuroImage 59:1783-1794
finding: Art students designed book-cover illustrations in an fMRI scanner on a drawing tablet and alternated between generating and evaluating ideas. Generation recruited medial temporal lobe regions. Evaluation recruited executive and default network regions together, plus rostrolateral PFC, insula and temporopolar cortex. Executive and default regions were positively coupled throughout.
numbers: Abstract only read this session (Europe PMC); full text and sample size not opened. A tracing control condition is described in a secondary review.
limits: Full text paywalled; the exact N, contrast thresholds and per-region statistics are not verified here. Single study, artists only, one domain.
agent_relevance: Founding evidence that producing and judging ideas use different neural configurations. Supports keeping generation and judging as separate calls (G5, G8), but see a12: later work shows the split is network cooperation, not two isolated modules.

source: Beaty, Benedek, Silvia, Schacter (2016) Creative cognition and brain network dynamics. Trends Cogn Sci 20:87-95
finding: Summarises the Ellamil study as: art students sketched book-cover ideas then evaluated them. Generation was associated with widespread default-region activity. Evaluation was associated with both default (MPFC, PCC) and control (DLPFC, ACC) activity, with increased default-control coupling during evaluation. Proposes that the default network proposes candidate ideas and the control network constrains them by top-down monitoring.
numbers: Describes the poetry study (Liu 2015) and the art study as both showing increased default-control coupling during evaluation. No new data.
quote: the default network influences the generation of candidate ideas, but that the control network can constrain and direct this process
limits: This secondary description of Ellamil differs from the abstract in emphasis (default regions for generation vs medial temporal lobe). Check the primary before quoting regions.
agent_relevance: Gives the working model: generation = loose associative proposal, evaluation = constrained control. A reason to give the judge call different instructions and no authorship, not just a second pass by the same prompt.

source: Liu, Erkkinen, Healey, Xu, Swett, Chow, Braun (2015) Brain activity and connectivity during poetry composition. Hum Brain Mapp 36:3351-3372
finding: Poets improvised new poems (generation) and then revised the same poems (revision) in the scanner. Generation increased medial PFC and decreased DLPFC, intraparietal sulcus and precuneus. Revision re-engaged DLPFC and IPS. Control is relaxed while generating and returns when revising.
numbers: 30 recruited, 27 analysed (14 expert MFA poets, 13 novices). Six tasks, four blocks of 60 s each, 17 s fixation. Generation vs memorised recitation, and vs random typing, gave essentially identical patterns. Network analysis used 53 independent components. Fluency tests did not differ between groups (e.g. F-A-S words 53 vs 50, p>0.05).
quote: cognitive control is attenuated during generation and re-engaged during revision
limits: Revision always followed generation (order fixed within session), so phase and order are confounded. Typing task, one genre. Experts showed stronger DLPFC/IPS deactivation during generation, but overall patterns were the same in both groups.
agent_relevance: Strongest simple demonstration that the same person switches control on and off between phases. Supports a hard phase boundary: no judging while generating, then a judging pass that sees the generated text.

source: Liu et al. (2015) poetry study: expert versus novice difference
finding: Experts suspended control more strongly during generation, but experts and novices used the same cognitive resources. Poem quality, rated by an independent expert panel, tracked different connectivity: medial PFC links for technical craft, DLPFC/IPS links for innovation.
numbers: Same 14 experts and 13 novices. Experts scored higher than novices on all craft and linguistic-creativity measures (t-tests, p<0.001 for most).
limits: Correlational connectivity-quality links in small groups.
agent_relevance: Quality depends on both modes, not on one. Suggests the judge should score craft and novelty separately rather than one blended score.

source: Beaty, Benedek, Kaufman, Silvia (2015) Default and executive network coupling supports creative idea production. Sci Rep 5:10964
finding: During an alternate-uses task (versus an object-characteristics control), a divergent-thinking network spanned default hubs (PCC, precuneus, inferior parietal) and executive DLPFC. Default-salience coupling came early in the trial and default-executive coupling later, so one trial moves from loose generation to control.
numbers: Original sample 28 young adults; independent resting-state sample n=42 used to confirm network membership. Trial: 12 s generation window per object, 3 s response. Network efficiency rose with divergent-thinking ability.
limits: Within one idea the stages are not cleanly separated; they overlap in time. Small sample. Does not show that evaluation is a separate process, only a later cooperation.
agent_relevance: Warns that the human split is soft: generation and control interleave inside a single idea. A scaffold should allow a short self-check inside generation only via code signals, not a model judging pass (G1, G5).

source: Benedek, Jauk, Fink, Koschutnig, Reishofer, Ebner, Neubauer (2014) To create or to recall? Neural mechanisms underlying the generation of creative new ideas. NeuroImage 88:125-133
finding: In self-paced spoken alternate-uses idea generation, left prefrontal and right medial temporal lobe were active and right temporoparietal junction deactivated. New ideas (vs recalled old ideas) activated left inferior parietal cortex. Orbital inferior frontal gyrus activity rose with idea creativity, read as executive control overcoming dominant responses.
numbers: N=35 (24 female), ages 18-29, after excluding 7. Mean 85.37 ideas each (SD 31.34); 48.34 old vs 37.02 new ideas. Old ideas came first and had shorter latency (6.69 vs 8.73 s, d=1.16); new ideas rated more creative (d=1.46). 15 task blocks of 60 s.
limits: Only the generation side is measured; evaluation is not separated. Original ideas appear later in the trial after memory-retrieved ones.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the serial order effect: early outputs are retrieved, later outputs are new. Supports sampling many ideas and discarding the first obvious ones, with code (not a model) deciding the cut.

source: Gonen-Yaacovi, de Souza, Levy, Urbanski, Josse, Volle (2013) Rostral and caudal prefrontal contribution to creativity: a meta-analysis of functional imaging data. Front Hum Neurosci 7:465
finding: Activation likelihood estimation across creativity tasks found a shared left-hemisphere set (caudal lateral PFC, medial and lateral rostral PFC, inferior parietal, posterior temporal). Lateral PFC showed a rostro-caudal axis: rostral regions for combining remote ideas, caudal regions for freely generating unusual responses.
numbers: 34 functional imaging studies in healthy adults. Verbal and non-verbal tasks shared left caudal prefrontal, temporal and parietal regions but also had domain-specific areas.
limits: Meta-analysis mostly of generation tasks; evaluation is barely represented in the pool. Task heterogeneity (insight, divergent thinking, music, metaphor).
agent_relevance: Shows that creative generation is itself at least two operations (free generation vs combination). Maps onto separate operators in a scaffold rather than one generic 'be creative' prompt.

source: Sowden, Pringle, Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory. Thinking & Reasoning 21:40-60
finding: Reviews dual-process models in creativity: generation vs evaluation maps only loosely onto Type 1 vs Type 2 thinking. Notes that Ellamil et al. found default and executive networks both active during evaluation but not during generation, and that the anterior insula/ACC salience network may switch between modes. Warns that rapid cycling can cause promising ideas to be evaluated too early.
numbers: Cites Jansson and Smith (1991) for harm from showing examples during generation, and Nijstad et al. (2010), Zabelina and Beeman (2013) for premature evaluation. Text word count 7,474.
quote: rapid cycling between modes of thinking may result in ideas being prematurely evaluated leading to promising ideas being dismissed
limits: A conceptual review; the cited behavioural effects were not re-checked here. Its description of Ellamil ('not during creative generation') is stronger than the abstract wording.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: do not interleave judging into the generation call, and shift modes on a code signal (salience analogue = impasse or check failure), not on a timer (G1).

source: Finke, Ward, Smith (1992) Creative Cognition (Geneplore model), as described in Sowden et al. 2015
finding: Geneplore splits creative thinking into a generate phase (retrieve items, associate, synthesise pre-inventive structures) and an explore phase (find attributes of the structures and test their possible functions). Generated ideas copy attributes of exemplars from the same domain.
numbers: Second-hand description. No numbers given in the review.
limits: Read only through Sowden et al.; the original book was not opened.
agent_relevance: The closest formal ancestor of S3 GENERATE then S4 TEST. Matches our states; explore phase = test against a function, which fits code-run checks.

source: Campbell (1960) and Simonton (1999-2012) Blind variation and selective retention, as described in Sowden et al. 2015
finding: BVSR: ideas are produced by blind variation and then selectively retained. Blind means the creator has no subjective certainty which variant leads toward the goal. The review notes BVSR assumes successive ideas are unrelated, which empirical work (Feinstein 2006; Nijstad and Stroebe 2006) does not support.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Described second-hand. Whether variation is truly blind is disputed.
agent_relevance: Formal justification for a generator that does not self-censor and a selector that works from outside evidence. The non-independence of successive ideas matches the correlated samples in G4.

source: Basadur (1982, 1995) ideation-evaluation cycles, as described in Sowden et al. 2015
finding: Creative work has three stages (problem finding, problem solving, implementation) and ideation and evaluation occur in cycles within each, in different ratios: problem finding is mostly ideation, implementation mostly evaluation. People differ in their tendency to ideate vs evaluate.
numbers: No numbers in the review.
limits: Second-hand. Style-difference claims depend on Basadur's own inventory.
agent_relevance: Suggests the generate/judge ratio should depend on the stage: wide ideation early, heavy checking late. A budget rule by state, not a fixed 1:1 split (G12).

source: Lloyd-Cox, Chen, Beaty (2022) The time course of creativity: multivariate classification of default and executive network contributions to creative cognition over time. Cortex
finding: Classifier accuracy for creative vs non-creative trials followed a U-shape over three time phases of one idea in both default and executive networks. Executive network accuracy was higher than default in early phases. Default-network activity predicted idea quality most in early phases and executive-network activity most in later phases. The authors call it tentative evidence for separate generative and evaluative stages.
numbers: Abstract only read this session; sample size and effect sizes not checked.
limits: The authors' own wording is tentative. Earlier executive involvement than expected conflicts with a clean generate-then-evaluate order.
agent_relevance: A direct test, and the result is hedged: stages exist but overlap. Treat the generate/judge split as a design choice we test at equal tokens (G7), not as a settled fact about brains.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Over-generate-and-rank agent with a separate LLM ranker: blind expert reviewers judged LLM ideas more novel than expert-human ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility. Generation worked; the LLM's own selection step did not (see a14, a15).
numbers: Per-review means: novelty human 4.84 (n=119 reviews), AI 5.64 (n=109), AI plus human rerank 5.81 (n=109); p<0.01. Feasibility 6.61 / 6.34 / 6.44 (not significant). 49 idea writers, 79 reviewers, nearly 300 reviews total.
limits: Reviewers disagree a lot (a15). Human ideas were written in 10 days and may be below the writers' best. One topic family (NLP prompting). Novelty judged on the idea text, not on results (see a17).
agent_relevance: Generation by a model can beat experts on judged novelty, but only reviewers outside the loop could tell. Supports G8: do not let the generator pick.

source: Si et al. (2024) LLM ranker and human reranking
finding: The Claude-3.5-Sonnet pairwise Swiss-tournament ranker picked top ideas that overlapped little with a human expert's reranking.
numbers: Zero-shot accept/reject accuracy on ICLR papers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4%, GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%; N=5 Swiss rounds chosen on validation. Only 17 of 49 ideas in the human-rerank condition were also top-ranked by the AI ranker.
limits: The 71.4% is on papers, not ideas; the ranker was tuned there then used on ideas.
agent_relevance: A selector validated on one object type does not transfer to another. Validate any judge on held-out items of the actual problem class (G3).

source: Si et al. (2024) LLMs cannot evaluate ideas reliably
finding: Ranking the top and bottom 25% of ideas by average expert score, every LLM evaluator was at or near chance and below human inter-reviewer agreement.
numbers: Balanced accuracy: random 50.0, NeurIPS 2021 reviewers 66.0, ICLR 2024 reviewers 71.9, this study's human reviewers 56.1, GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3.
limits: Human ground truth itself is noisy (56.1%), which caps any judge. Authors warn that matching human agreement would not prove validity.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G8: a model judge of ideas is near chance. Human agreement on idea quality is also low, so a code-run check is the only firm selector.

source: Si et al. (2024) Diversity ceiling of LLM idea generation
finding: Over-generation stops paying: duplicates dominate as more ideas are sampled, so the pool for any selector stops growing.
numbers: 4,000 seed ideas per topic, embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), duplicate if cosine similarity above 0.8: only about 200 non-duplicate ideas out of 4,000.
limits: Threshold of 0.8 is a choice; one agent and prompt design.
agent_relevance: Cap the number of samples and spend the rest on a diversity step. Matches G12 (do not resample heavily without a foothold) and gives a measurable stop rule in code.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap: execution outcomes of LLM-generated versus human research ideas
finding: When 43 expert researchers actually executed randomly assigned LLM or human ideas, the LLM ideas lost their ideation-stage advantage. Scores of LLM ideas dropped significantly more than human ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall (p<0.05), and rankings flipped on many metrics.
numbers: 43 executors, average 103 hours each, 4-page papers reviewed blind. Effectiveness: AI ideas 6.00 before to 4.13 after (N=24); human ideas 4.83 to 4.78 (N=19). Correlation between ideation and execution scores was weak, and moderately negative for AI ideas on excitement.
limits: Final AI-below-human difference was not statistically significant. NLP prompting research only; executors adapted ideas (changed datasets, models, metrics).
agent_relevance: Judging an idea by reading it, even by experts, is a poor proxy for running it. Strongest support for G8: novelty and merit are judged by execution or a check, not by an opinion call.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet. ICLR
finding: Apparent self-correction gains come from oracle labels that tell the model when to stop. With no oracle, the same model critiquing and revising its own answer is flat or worse.
numbers: With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5. Intrinsic (no oracle): GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 (41.8 after round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 then 89.0. Debate no better than self-consistency at equal responses.
limits: Reasoning tasks with a single right answer; not creative evaluation. Some gain claims traced to weak initial prompts.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G5: revise only from a real external signal, never from the model's own verdict. Also supports G9 (no debate).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: One LLM generates, gives feedback on its own output, then refines it, up to four rounds, on 7 tasks including dialogue, code optimisation, sentiment reversal, acronym and constrained generation. Authors report outputs preferred by humans and metrics over one-step output.
numbers: About 20% absolute average task improvement (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4). Up to 4 iterations. Feedback and refine done as few-shot prompts.
limits: Counter-evidence to Huang et al. (a18): gains are on tasks with graded, checkable outputs and the same model gives and receives feedback, which a21 predicts is biased.
agent_relevance: A separate feedback call does help on checkable tasks. Keep it only where code can score the revision (G3, G7), and test at equal tokens.

source: Yao, Yu, Zhao, Shafran, Griffiths, Cao, Narasimhan (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: Splitting thought generation (propose k candidates) from state evaluation (value or vote by a separate prompt), with search over states, sharply beats single-chain prompting on Game of 24. For creative writing, evaluation by vote chooses among plans.
numbers: Game of 24: input-output 7.3%, chain-of-thought 4.0%, CoT self-consistency 9.0%, ToT breadth 1 = 45%, breadth 5 = 74%; best of 100 CoT = 49%. About 60% of CoT samples already failed after the first step. Creative writing GPT-4 coherency: refine step raised IO 6.19 to 7.67 and ToT 7.56 to 7.91.
limits: Game of 24 values are easy to check by arithmetic, so evaluation is accurate there; creative writing used GPT-4 as scorer (self-judging). Cost much higher than CoT.
agent_relevance: Shows a separate evaluator call can work when it is checkable. It is a design precedent for S3/S4, but the evaluator's quality, not the split itself, decides the gain.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations
finding: LLMs can recognise their own text, and the stronger that recognition, the more they prefer their own outputs when judging. So a judge that sees the generator's authorship is biased toward it.
numbers: GPT-4 identifies itself from two other LLMs and humans at 73.5% out of the box. GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 exceed 90% self-recognition after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Self-preference scales linearly with self-recognition (fine-tuning to raise or lower it).
limits: Summarisation tasks (CNN/DailyMail, XSUM); not creative ideas. Causal claim rests on fine-tuning interventions.
agent_relevance: Reason to strip authorship and style cues before a judging call, and ideally to use a different model or code as selector (G5, G8).

source: West, Lu, Dziri, Brahman, Li, et al. (2023) The generative AI paradox: what it can create, it may not understand
finding: Generative models often match or beat people at generating but fall short at selecting or answering questions about the same type of output. In humans understanding is a prerequisite of expert generation; in models it is not.
numbers: Vision selection example: human discrimination 92.86-100% across COCO, PaintSkill, T2ICompBench, DrawBench, Midjourney; CLIP variants about 72-88% on the same sets. Model-human gap grows with task difficulty. Language: GPT-4 discrimination weaker than human and less tied to its own generation quality.
limits: Preprint; tasks are constrained generation and image-text matching, not creativity. It compares model with human, not two phases.
agent_relevance: Predicts that a model is a better generator than judge, which is why selection should not rest on its judging call (G5, G8). Human-style ability to recognise a good idea cannot be assumed.

source: Zhang, Diddee, Holm, Liu, Liu, Samuel, Wang, Ippolito (2025) NoveltyBench: evaluating language models for humanlike diversity. COLM
finding: Across 20 leading models, generation diversity is well below human writers, and larger models within a family are often less diverse than smaller ones. In-context regeneration helps. Quality is scored by a reward model, so it measures generation spread, not a judge.
numbers: Average distinct generations per prompt (higher is more diverse): Claude-3.5 Sonnet 1.76, Claude-3.5 Haiku 1.94, gpt-4o 2.88, gpt-4o-mini 2.65, Llama-3.1-405B 3.20, gemma-2-2b 5.66, Llama-3.2-1B 6.74 (with lower utility 2.81). Utility scored 1-10 by Skywork reward model calibrated to GPT-4.
limits: Distinctness is from a learned classifier; small models are more diverse partly because they are worse. Does not test generate-then-judge directly.
agent_relevance: The generator's pool is narrow, so a separate selector has little to choose from; diversity must come from the generation side (separate sampling, regeneration with prior answers shown), then judging. Links to our NoveltyBench A/B.

source: Sowden et al. (2015) on example exposure and premature evaluation, citing Jansson and Smith (1991), Nijstad et al. (2010), Zabelina and Beeman (2013)
finding: Behavioural findings cited by the review: presenting examples during a generative phase harms creative output (Jansson and Smith 1991), and switching to judging too early causes promising ideas to be dropped.
numbers: No numbers reported in the review.
limits: Second-hand; original studies not opened. Fixation effect itself has mixed replication.
agent_relevance: Two concrete rules for the generation call: no prior solutions in the prompt (or few, deliberately), and no judgement language. Can be tested as an A/B on mixed vs separate prompts.

source: Andrews-Hanna, Smallwood, Spreng (2014) The default network and self-generated thought. Ann NY Acad Sci
finding: Frontoparietal control network interacts with default and dorsal attention networks during tasks that need maintenance and extended evaluation of internal information in service of a goal. This is the general account in which creative evaluation is one case of evaluating self-generated thought.
numbers: No creativity-specific numbers; cites Ellamil et al. in the reference list (ref 168).
limits: A general review, not a creativity test.
agent_relevance: Frames evaluation as control over internally generated content. Analogue for an agent: the judge should receive the generated content as external data, with the goal restated.

source: Beaty, Kenett, Christensen, Rosenberg, Benedek, Chen, Fink, Qiu, Kwapil, Kane, Silvia (2018) Robust prediction of individual creative ability from brain functional connectivity. PNAS
finding: A connectome-based model built from default, executive and salience network connections predicted individual creative ability in independent samples, tying creative performance to coupling of generation-like and control-like networks rather than to either alone.
numbers: Only the bibliographic header was retrieved this session; sample sizes and r values not verified. The finding is stated from memory of the paper's abstract.
limits: Not opened beyond metadata; verify before quoting.
agent_relevance: Indirect support for the cooperation view. Include only after opening the paper.

source: Beaty et al. (2019) Network neuroscience of creative cognition (review)
finding: Review whose reference list cites Ellamil et al. (2012) as part of the evidence for default and control network cooperation in creative thought.
numbers: Only the Ellamil citation was confirmed in the text read; no figures extracted.
limits: Claims of the review not verified.
agent_relevance: Pointer for forward citation search, not evidence in itself.
